Chairman of the Petrograd Soviet in 1917

stem: What was a show trial in Stalin's USSR?

options.content: A trial in which the jury was chosen by the accused themselves
A secret trial with no record kept

stem: Which evidence best suggests that Stalin's control was NOT total by 1941?

stem: Describe how Stalin used propaganda to strengthen his control.

points.description: Cult of personality: portraits, statues, praise in newspapers; towns named after him.
History rewritten to exaggerate his role (official party history, 1938).
Photographs altered to remove purged leaders.
Culture controlled: socialist realism; art and literature glorified Stalin and socialism.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Stalin built a cult of personality: his portraits and statues were everywhere, newspapers praised him as the father of the peoples and towns such as Stalingrad were named after him. History was rewritten to exaggerate his role in 1917, and photographs were altered to remove leaders who had been purged. Writers, artists and composers had to follow socialist realism, producing optimistic works that glorified socialism and Stalin.

stem: Explain why Stalin launched the Purges.

points.description: Identifies removing potential rivals.
Explains that Old Bolsheviks who knew of Lenin's criticisms could challenge him, so they were eliminated in show trials.
Identifies creating fear / scapegoats.
Explains that terror made opposition impossible and blamed 'wreckers' for economic failures.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Stalin wanted to remove anyone who might challenge him, especially Old Bolsheviks such as Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin who remembered Lenin's criticisms and could become leaders of opposition; show trials eliminated and discredited them. The Purges also created fear, so that no one dared to resist, and provided scapegoats: failures in the Five-Year Plans could be blamed on 'wreckers' and 'saboteurs'.

hints: Think about threats to Stalin and the uses of fear.

stem: Explain why Stalin, and not Trotsky, became leader of the Soviet Union.

points.description: Identifies the General Secretary's power.
Explains that control of appointments gave Stalin supporters who voted for him at party congresses.
Identifies Stalin's political skill / popular policy.
Explains alliances with each group in turn and the appeal of Socialism in One Country.
Identifies Trotsky's weaknesses.
Explains arrogance, late membership, fear of him as a military dictator, missing Lenin's funeral, failure to build alliances.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: As General Secretary, Stalin controlled appointments to party posts, so local officials owed their jobs to him and voted for him at party congresses. He was a skilful politician who allied with Zinoviev and Kamenev against Trotsky, then with Bukharin against them, and finally turned on Bukharin. His policy of Socialism in One Country appealed to party members tired of upheaval. Trotsky, by contrast, seemed arrogant, had joined the Bolsheviks only in 1917, and was feared as a possible military dictator; he missed Lenin's funeral and failed to build alliances or to use Lenin's Testament against Stalin.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a description in words of a Soviet poster of the kind produced in the late 1930s (described in words; invented for this question)

> Stalin, smiling and dressed in a plain military tunic, holds a small girl who offers him a bunch of flowers. Behind them, crowds carry red banners past new factories. The caption reads: 'Thank you, dear Stalin, for our happy childhood!'

**Source B** — an account written in 1960 by a fictional former engineer who had been arrested in 1937 (invented for this question)

> They came at night, as they always did. My crime, I learned after months of questioning, was that a machine in my workshop had broken down. I signed what they put in front of me. In the camp I met teachers, party secretaries, a priest and a peasant who had complained about the collective farm. None of us had done anything.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What is the message of Source A?

points.description: Stalin is a kind, loving father figure (cult of personality).
Life in the USSR is happy and prosperous thanks to him (new factories).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far does Source B challenge the view given in Source A?

points.description: B shows terror and arbitrary arrest, the opposite of A's happiness.
B shows innocent people from all groups imprisoned; A shows a contented people.
B shows forced confessions; A shows love for Stalin.
They are not wholly contradictory: A shows the propaganda that hid what B describes / both show the regime's control.

parts.explanation: Points of challenge, with an explanation of how both can be true.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How useful are these sources for understanding how Stalin controlled the Soviet Union? Use the sources and your own knowledge.

points.description: A: useful evidence of propaganda and the cult of personality (purpose: build loyalty).
A: tells us nothing reliable about real feelings; designed to hide reality.
B: useful for terror: night arrests, forced confessions, the Gulag, victims from many groups (own knowledge: 1937-38).
B: written in 1960, after Stalin's death, by a victim; may be bitter but details match archive evidence.
Together they show the two main methods: propaganda and terror.
Supported judgement.

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source A is useful as evidence of propaganda: it shows the cult of personality, presenting Stalin as a loving father who has brought happiness and progress. Its purpose was to build loyalty, so it tells us what the regime wanted people to believe, not how they really felt. Source B is useful as evidence of terror: night arrests, a forced confession, and a camp full of teachers, party secretaries, a priest and a peasant, which matches what historians know of the Great Terror of 1937-38 and the Gulag. It was written in 1960 by a former victim and may be bitter, but its details fit archive evidence. Together the sources are very useful because they show the two main methods of control, propaganda and terror, although neither covers the purges of the party leadership and army or the role of the NKVD in detail.

parts.explanation: Usefulness from content, provenance and own knowledge.

hints: Consider when, why and by whom each source was produced.

parts.stem: How complete was Stalin's control of the Soviet Union by 1941?

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Stalin's political control was almost complete by 1941. All his former rivals had been killed or exiled, and Trotsky was murdered in 1940. The show trials and the purge of the army had removed anyone who might challenge him, and the party, army and NKVD were filled with people who owed their careers to him. Terror, carried out by the NKVD and the Gulag, made open opposition almost impossible, while the cult of personality, rewritten history and socialist realism shaped what people saw and read.

However, control was less complete in practice. The Terror caused chaos: managers and officers were arrested, the economy and army were weakened, and officials sometimes bent or ignored instructions to protect themselves. Peasants resisted quietly by working slowly on the collective farms or hiding grain, and many people kept their religious faith and private opinions.

Overall Stalin's control over politics was total, but his control over society was not: people obeyed out of fear and habit rather than full belief, and the regime's own methods created disorder.

parts.explanation: Levels: both sides with a supported judgement for the top level.

hints: In (b), consider political power, the economy, and people's private lives.
